profiles.name: MEDLEY
profiles.synopsis: A symmetric encryption primitive exposed through familiar block-cipher modes.

facts.text: Viasat advertises MEDLEY-256 with GCM, CTR, OFB and CFB.
Standard GCM uses a 128-bit block cipher and does not use its inverse function.
The NGLD-M requirements list MEDLEY for data-at-rest and non-security software confidentiality.

inferences.text: The advertised GCM profile implies a keyed 128-bit block permutation interface.
inferences.assumption: GCM denotes the standard NIST mode.

inferences.text: The advertised modes can process message encryption and decryption using only the forward block-cipher function.
inferences.assumption: The modes follow their standard definitions; see S004 sections 6.3-6.5.

inferences.text: The -256 designation suggests a 256-bit key variant, but does not by itself establish entropy or attack cost.

unknowns: Round function, key schedule and relationship to AES are not established by these records.
The original 2001 mode set need not equal the later advertised mode set.

profiles.name: BATON
profiles.synopsis: A block-oriented cipher with structured key representation and token-controlled initialization.

facts.text: PKCS #11 encodes a BATON key value in 40 bytes and identifies 160 bits as checksum material.
Named mechanisms include ECB128, ECB96, CBC128, COUNTER, SHUFFLE and WRAP; encryption-mode IV parameters are 24 bytes and token-selected.
NSA described BATON as supporting higher throughput than SKIPJACK with then-current microelectronics.

inferences.text: If the checksum bits are determined by the remaining bits, this encoding contains at most 160 independent key bits: 320 minus 160.
inferences.assumption: The checksum is deterministic from the remaining encoded key material.

inferences.text: The interface places encryption initialization policy inside the device.

unknowns: The entropy bound is not a demonstrated cryptanalytic attack cost.
The 192-bit IV parameter does not establish a 192-bit block size or internal state size.

profiles.name: JUNIPER
profiles.synopsis: A historical block-cipher interface closely resembling BATON at the API boundary.

facts.text: JUNIPER has a 40-byte key representation containing 160 checksum bits, with ECB128, CBC128, counter, shuffle and wrapping mechanisms.
A public JUNIPER mechanism description appears in the December 1999 PKCS #11 standard.

inferences.text: Shared key-format and mechanism conventions support reuse of integration infrastructure.

unknowns: A common API does not establish a common round function, key schedule or design ancestry.

profiles.name: ACCORDION
profiles.synopsis: A versioned key-protection mechanism in the key-management path.

facts.text: ACCORDION 1.3 is assigned transfer-key protection and acceptable internal key wrapping.
ACCORDION 3.0 is an internal wrapping option and appears as a future KMI black-key wrapping option in the 2019 table.
A 2002 reference is titled NSA MEDLEY Implementation Standard: An ACCORDION MEDLEY.

inferences.text: A useful abstract interface is a wrapping key plus key material producing a protected key object.
The MEDLEY-related title is evidence of a documented relationship, whose construction remains unspecified.

unknowns: The cited roles do not expose a complete primitive or wrapping encoding.
A future requirement is not evidence that a feature shipped.

profiles.name: JOSEKI
profiles.synopsis: Confidentiality for loadable algorithm software in a protected execution environment.

facts.text: AIM tooling includes a JOSEKI encryptor for preparing program code and a JOSEKI decryption service.

source_refs.locator: p.2, software environment and SOS services

facts.text: AIM requires properly digitally signed software.
Harris lists JOSEKI Decrypt among Sierra II capabilities.

inferences.text: The documented tools support protected software preparation, distribution and device-side loading.

source_refs.locator: p.2, software environment and SOS services

inferences.text: A decrypt-only product entry describes its role as a recipient; it does not identify the cipher as asymmetric.

source_refs.locator: p.2, software environment and SOS services

unknowns: Package format, key schedule and the ordering of decryption and signature checks are not specified here.

profiles.name: WATARI
profiles.synopsis: A confidentiality mechanism for security-software delivery.

facts.text: NGLD-M assigns WATARI to security-software confidentiality and includes it among non-security software options.

inferences.text: WATARI protects the contents of software packages in this deployment model.

unknowns: A related purpose does not establish that WATARI derives from JOSEKI.
Its internal mathematical construction is not established by the role assignment.

profiles.name: FIREFLY / Enhanced FIREFLY
profiles.synopsis: Endpoint key establishment rather than the bulk data-processing stage.

facts.text: The KIV-19M brochure describes establishing a unique encryption key over full-duplex channels without an online third party.
Diffie discussed FIREFLY in 1988 and considered an exponentiation-based construction plausible from contemporary descriptions and testimony.
NSA history identifies FIREFLY as a public-key algorithm underpinning STU-III.

source_refs.locator: Printed p.297; PDF p.40, STU-III discussion

inferences.text: The scheme belongs in the stage that establishes shared key material for later traffic protection.
Classical exponentiation-based public-key mathematics is a historically grounded hypothesis, not a released specification.

unknowns: An exact identification with Diffie-Hellman, RSA or a particular authenticated variant is not established.
No online third party does not imply no provisioning, certificates or prior trust.

profiles.name: SPONDULIX-S

facts.text: NGLD-M lists SPONDULIX-S alongside ECDH-384 under KMI key agreement.

inferences.text: It occupies a key-establishment role in KMI.

unknowns: Being listed beside ECDH-384 does not establish identical mathematics, curve parameters or strength.
First development and first approval dates have not been verified.

profiles.name: KM-TG signing schemes / SILVER LINING
profiles.synopsis: Authorization and authenticity checks for software updates.

facts.text: NGLD-M describes NSA-signed security-software updates and device-side validation using KM-TG schemes, with an upgrade path to SILVER LINING.

inferences.text: These schemes establish whether software is accepted as authorized; confidentiality is a separate function in the same update process.

unknowns: The record does not identify SILVER LINING as RSA, elliptic-curve or hash-based signatures.
The planned transition is not a verified first operational approval date.

profiles.name: SAVILLE
profiles.synopsis: An older secure-voice lineage with a measurable implementation cost on AIM.

facts.text: NSA history dates the SAVILLE tactical secure-voice program to the late 1960s and associates VINSON with the family.

source_refs.locator: Printed p.143; PDF p.154, tactical secure-voice discussion

facts.text: Motorola advertises SAVILLE at 0.04 bits per input clock and BATON at 1.29 bits per input clock on AIM.

inferences.text: Applying the advertised rates at a hypothetical 10 MHz input clock gives 0.4 Mbps for SAVILLE and 12.9 Mbps for BATON, a 32.25-fold throughput ratio.
The ratio measures implementation cost on that platform, combining algorithm, mode and implementation choices.

unknowns: These performance figures do not identify the internal feedback structure, round count or security margin.
Detailed online reconstructions require separate evidence from an original design record.
